chapters.title: Chapter 2: Ensemble Methods I: Bagging and Boosting

lessons.title: Reading the Model's Mind: Feature Importance and SHAP for Trading Signals

body.text: A model you cannot explain is a model you cannot size real capital behind, and more importantly, a model whose overfitting you cannot catch before it costs you. SHAP is this course's answer to both problems at once: it turns a black-box ensemble into something you can defend to a risk committee, and something you can audit for exactly the leakage Chapter 1 warned about.

children.text: Why Feature Importance Alone Isn't Enough

Every tree ensemble ships with a built-in feature importance ranking, and every version of it has the same core limitation: it is a single global number per feature. It cannot tell you whether a feature's effect on a specific prediction was positive or negative, whether that effect makes economic sense, or how two features interact with each other, exactly the value-and-quality-trend interaction the previous chapter used to motivate ML as a combination layer in the first place.

body.caption: Three common feature importance methods, and where each falls short

cells: Average improvement in split quality a feature contributes across all trees
Biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features; no sense of direction
How often a feature is used to split, anywhere in the ensemble
Even more biased toward features with many possible split points; ignores how much each split actually helped
Drop in model performance when a feature's values are shuffled
Model-agnostic and more reliable than the two above, but still a single global number, with no per-prediction or interaction detail

body.text: What you actually want to know is not just which features matter on average, but why the model made this specific prediction, for this specific stock, on this specific day, and whether that reasoning survives basic economic scrutiny. That is a different question, and it needs a different tool.

children.text: SHAP: A Principled Way to Attribute Predictions

markDefs.definition: A method for attributing a model's prediction to its input features, grounded in Shapley values from cooperative game theory, which fairly splits a total payoff among players based on their average marginal contribution across every possible order they could join in.

children.text: SHAP, short for SHapley Additive exPlanations, treats each feature like a player in a cooperative game where the payoff is the model's prediction. A feature's

is its fair share of the credit for pushing the prediction away from the average, computed by averaging its marginal contribution across every possible order features could be added in. Computed naively this is combinatorially expensive, but TreeSHAP, the algorithm this course uses throughout, computes exact SHAP values for tree ensembles in polynomial time, which is what makes this practical to run on every prediction a random forest or gradient booster makes, not just a handful of examples.

body.caption: A prediction's SHAP values, φᵢ for each of M features, always sum exactly to the gap between that prediction, f(x), and the model's average prediction across the dataset, E[f(X)]. This efficiency property is what makes SHAP values reconcile precisely, not just look plausible.

body.label: The SHAP Guarantee
body.context: Every prediction's feature contributions add up perfectly to the actual output. That reconciling property is what separates SHAP from a plausible-looking importance ranking.

children.text: A SHAP summary, or beeswarm, plot puts every prediction's SHAP value for a given feature as a single dot, colored by whether that feature's value was high or low for that row, with features stacked top to bottom by mean absolute SHAP impact. Read correctly, it tells you two things a bar chart of feature importance cannot: which features matter most, and whether high values of each feature push predictions up or down. A momentum feature where high values consistently push predictions toward the 'up' label is behaving exactly as economic theory predicts. A feature where high and low values are scattered on both sides with no clear pattern is probably closer to noise than signal, regardless of how highly it ranks on a plain importance chart.

body.title: Illustrative: Mean |SHAP Value| by Feature for a Next-Day Direction Classifier

body.text: These SHAP magnitudes are an illustrative example built to show how a ranking is read, not output from an actual trained model. The next lesson's case study reports real feature attributions for a specific gradient-boosted signal.

children.text: Using SHAP to Catch Overfitting and Leakage, Not Just to Explain

SHAP's most valuable job on a trading desk is not explaining a good model, it is catching a broken one before it goes live. If one feature's mean |SHAP| value dwarfs every other feature combined, and the model's walk-forward accuracy is unusually high, that combination should make you more suspicious, not more confident. It is the same warning sign as the 91% accuracy number from Chapter 1's first lesson, just visible through a different window: the most likely explanation is that the feature is leaking label information, directly or through an indirect correlation, rather than reflecting a genuinely dominant economic driver.

body.text: A single feature dominating a SHAP summary plot is not automatically a discovery. Check it for leakage first: was it computed using any information that would not have been available at the actual decision time? Only once that is ruled out does it become a genuinely interesting result worth investigating further.

children.text: SHAP Interaction Values: Catching What Feature Importance Rankings Miss

TreeSHAP extends to interaction values, decomposing each pair of features' joint contribution separately from their individual effects. This is the tool that actually verifies whether a tree ensemble learned the value-times-quality-trend interaction the previous chapter used as its motivating example for ML as a combination layer, rather than you simply assuming it did because the model's overall accuracy looked reasonable. If cheap-and-improving stocks and cheap-and-deteriorating stocks are genuinely being treated differently, a value-quality interaction term shows up clearly in the interaction values. If they are not, the model may be leaning on value or quality independently, and the more interesting nonlinear story you were hoping for is not actually there.

body.code:
import shap

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
shap_values = explainer(X_val)   # an Explanation object, one row per prediction

# Global ranking, the number behind the bar chart above
import numpy as np
mean_abs_shap = np.abs(shap_values.values).mean(axis=0)
ranking = sorted(zip(X_val.columns, mean_abs_shap), key=lambda t: -t[1])

shap.plots.beeswarm(shap_values)          # per-prediction direction and spread
shap.plots.bar(shap_values)               # the plain global ranking
body.caption: shap.TreeExplainer is exact and fast for tree ensembles specifically; do not reach for the slower, sampling-based general Explainer when your model is a random forest or a gradient booster.

children.text: This chapter's closing case study puts everything from these three lessons together: a gradient-boosted momentum signal on the Nifty 200, built with triple-barrier labels, tuned with a chronological early-stopping split, and audited with SHAP before a single rupee of the walk-forward result is trusted.

body.title: Using the SHAP Efficiency Property
body.prompt: A model's average prediction across the training set is 0.50. For a specific stock, the model predicts 0.68. Three of the four features driving this prediction have SHAP values of +0.05, +0.03, and +0.02. Given that SHAP values must sum to the gap between this prediction and the baseline, what must the fourth feature's SHAP value be?
body.explanation: SHAP values always sum exactly to f(x) − E[f(X)] = 0.68 − 0.50 = 0.18. The three known contributions sum to 0.05 + 0.03 + 0.02 = 0.10, so the fourth feature's SHAP value must be 0.18 − 0.10 = 0.08. This efficiency property is what makes SHAP values additive and auditable in a way raw feature importance rankings are not.

body.title: A Suspicious SHAP Plot
body.question: In a SHAP summary plot for a next-day direction classifier, one single feature accounts for far more mean |SHAP| impact than all other features combined, more than double the next-highest feature, and the model's walk-forward accuracy is unusually high. What should you check first?
options: Whether that feature deserves a bigger position size in the final portfolio
Whether that feature could be leaking label information, such as being computed using data from after the point the label is decided
Whether the SHAP library is installed correctly
Whether the feature should be renamed for clarity
body.explanation: A single feature dominating SHAP importance this heavily, combined with unusually high accuracy, is the same red flag as the suspiciously high accuracy number covered in Chapter 1: the most likely explanation is that the feature is not really predictive so much as it is leaking information about the label, directly or through an indirect correlation, computed using data that would not actually have been available at decision time. SHAP does not just explain a good model, it is one of the fastest ways to catch a broken one.

points: Built-in feature importance methods, gain, split count, and permutation importance, each give a single global number per feature, with no sense of direction, per-prediction detail, or interactions
SHAP values are grounded in Shapley values from game theory and satisfy an efficiency property: they sum exactly to the gap between a prediction and the model's average prediction
TreeSHAP computes exact SHAP values for tree ensembles quickly enough to run on every prediction, which is what makes it practical for this course's models
A SHAP summary plot shows both importance and direction, letting you check whether a feature's effect makes economic sense, not just how large it is
A single feature dominating SHAP importance alongside unusually high accuracy is a leakage red flag first and a discovery second, echoing Chapter 1's warning about suspiciously high accuracy numbers
SHAP interaction values are the tool that actually confirms whether a tree ensemble learned a genuine feature interaction, like value combined with quality trend, rather than you assuming it did
